interview_metadata.name: Joseph Giordano
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Greensboro, North Carolina, in a pretty steady Italian-American family. My grandparents came over from southern Italy, and even though I grew up very much Southern, Sundays still meant pasta, Catholic church sometimes, and everybody respecting the older folks. I was a quiet kid. I liked taking things apart more than talking in big groups, so model trains, little electronics kits, and helping my dad in the garage were more my speed. School was okay for me, but I was never the guy who wanted four years of college just to sit in an office. After high school I did some community college classes and started leaning hard toward electrical work because it made sense to me: codes, diagrams, routines, and something useful at the end of the day. I am 21 now, never married, no kids, and working as an electrician, mostly residential wiring and troubleshooting. A big thing for me is trying to get licensed as a journeyman and eventually master electrician. I keep my life pretty simple: work, save money, take care of my back, fish or hike when I can, build small furniture, and spend time with family without making a big production out of everything.

follow_ups.question: What was your household like when you were growing up?
follow_ups.response: Pretty structured. My parents expected me to help, be respectful, and not waste money. We ate together a lot, especially on weekends, and my grandparents were around enough that family history was always kind of present.

follow_ups.question: Was there a childhood memory that still shapes how you live now?
follow_ups.response: My granddad had this habit of measuring twice before he cut anything, and he would say it like it was a rule for life. That stuck with me, especially in electrical work where rushing can hurt somebody.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The main crossroads was after high school. I had people telling me to keep going with college, and I did take some classes, but I could feel myself getting restless. Around that time I helped a friend's uncle on a residential job, mostly cleaning up, pulling wire, and watching how they laid everything out. It clicked for me in a way classroom work did not. I liked that there was a right way to do things and that you could learn from people who had done it for years. I chose to pursue electrical work instead of drifting through school without a clear plan. It made me more disciplined because now every hour I put in connects to getting licensed and eventually running my own small shop.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced that decision the most?
follow_ups.response: My dad supported it once he saw I was serious. He was practical about it and said a trade can give you a real living if you show up and learn.

follow_ups.question: What was hard about choosing that path?
follow_ups.response: I worried people would think I quit college because I could not handle it. Really it was more that I wanted a clear skill and a stable routine.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I remember sitting in my truck after class one day and thinking I could either keep paying for classes without direction or start building hours toward a license.

follow_ups.question: Did you write out a plan?
follow_ups.response: Yes, not fancy, just notes about apprenticeship hours, tools I needed, and what exams I would eventually have to pass.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel sure right away?
follow_ups.response: Not completely, but once I started working regularly, it felt right.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A better trade counseling setup in high school would have helped. I had to piece together information about licensing, pay, and apprenticeship routes mostly by asking around.

follow_ups.question: What would that help have looked like?
follow_ups.response: Someone explaining the path clearly: helper, apprentice, journeyman, master, and what the timeline costs.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help informally?
follow_ups.response: Yes, older electricians on jobs gave me practical advice, especially about tools and not hurting my back.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children. I have never been married. My parents are important to me, and I still see them often because they are here in Greensboro. My grandparents are a big part of the family story too, even when I do not see them every week. We are not the kind of family that talks feelings all day, but people show up with food, help with a repair, or check whether your truck is running right. I usually go over for Sunday dinner a couple times a month, and holidays are pretty family-centered. I also have a younger sister I am close to in a quiet way. We text more than we talk on the phone.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do when you see your family?
follow_ups.response: Mostly eat, help with little projects, and sit around talking about work, sports, or whatever needs fixing.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call first if something goes wrong?
follow_ups.response: Usually my dad for practical stuff, and my mom if I am stressed and need someone calmer.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My younger sister, Mia, is the main one. She is a little more social than me, but we get along and I help her with car or apartment stuff when she asks.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see her?
follow_ups.response: Maybe every other week, more around family dinners.

follow_ups.question: Do you two share interests?
follow_ups.response: Not many, but she likes some of the old records I play.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small circle. A coworker named Tyler is probably my closest friend right now because we are on job sites together and sometimes go fishing. I also know a couple guys from the gym, but that is more casual. I am not dating anybody seriously. I like people, but I need a lot of time alone after work, so I do better with low-pressure friendships.

follow_ups.question: How often do you hang out with Tyler outside work?
follow_ups.response: Maybe twice a month, usually fishing early on a Saturday or watching a Panthers game.

follow_ups.question: What makes a friendship work for you?
follow_ups.response: No drama, no constant texting, just showing up when it matters.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Greensboro, in the 27408 area. It is a mix of older houses, apartments, small shops, and places you can get to without driving too far. I like that it is not too loud, but it is still close to work supply stores, grocery stores, and my family. There are some nice tree-lined streets and older homes where you can tell people have been fixing things up over time. It feels practical, which suits me.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually shop nearby?
follow_ups.response: A regular grocery store, hardware stores, and electrical supply places when I need something specific.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by name. We wave, maybe talk about yard work, but I keep to myself.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock my truck and do not leave tools visible, but I am not afraid walking around during the day or coming home from work.

follow_ups.question: Have you had anything stolen?
follow_ups.response: No major theft, but I have heard of tools getting taken around town, so I am careful.

follow_ups.question: Do you walk at night?
follow_ups.response: Not much. If I want exercise, I usually go to the gym or hike somewhere.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and being near family. The downside is rent is not cheap, traffic can be annoying, and some areas feel like they are getting more expensive faster than wages.

follow_ups.question: Would you stay long term?
follow_ups.response: Probably in the Greensboro area, yes, though I would like a small house with a garage eventually.

follow_ups.question: What would make the area better?
follow_ups.response: More affordable starter homes and better options for young tradespeople.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now I live with one roommate, Tyler, who is also a coworker. It is mostly a practical arrangement so rent and utilities are manageable. We both work early, so the apartment stays pretty quiet. We split chores without a big system: I handle a lot of the small repairs and he usually deals with trash and some cleaning.

follow_ups.question: Do you share meals?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. We might grill on a weekend, but most nights we cook separately.

follow_ups.question: How is the living arrangement working?
follow_ups.response: It works because we both keep things simple and respect each other's space.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent for the current lease. It is just me and Tyler.

follow_ups.question: How long is the lease?
follow_ups.response: One year.

follow_ups.question: Any plans to change it?
follow_ups.response: Not unless rent jumps too much.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one stays regularly. Family might stop by, but not overnight much.

follow_ups.question: Any frequent visitors?
follow_ups.response: Not really.

follow_ups.question: Does Tyler have guests often?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, but it is not constant.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody is away like that.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is two?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: No one away at school?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are pretty steady. I get up around 5:45, pack lunch if I remembered to prep it, and get to the job site or shop by 7. Work runs until about 3:30 or 4:30, depending on the job. After work I might stop for supplies, go to the gym for light lifting, or head home and cook something simple. Saturdays are for errands, woodworking, fishing, or hiking if the weather is good. Sundays are quieter: laundry, family dinner sometimes, and getting ready for Monday.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10 if I am being smart, sometimes later if I get stuck working on a project.

follow_ups.question: What is your most predictable day?
follow_ups.response: Monday through Thursday are the most predictable because work sets the rhythm.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as an electrician, mostly residential. That means wiring new rooms, troubleshooting circuits, installing fixtures, checking panels, and making sure things line up with code. I am also getting some exposure to solar PV installs, which I really like because it feels like where the trade is going. My schedule is usually Monday through Friday, starting around 7 in the morning. Sometimes there is a Saturday job if a customer needs it or a project is behind.

follow_ups.question: What task do you like most?
follow_ups.response: Troubleshooting. I like tracing a problem and finding the one bad connection or overloaded circuit.

follow_ups.question: What task is hardest on you?
follow_ups.response: Crawlspaces and attic work, especially in heat. That is where my back gets irritated.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a small vegetable garden with tomatoes, basil, and zucchini, so I water that before or after work depending on the weather. I also budget every Sunday night, nothing complicated, just checking bills and savings. I try to stretch my back most nights because if I skip that for a week, I feel it. And I maintain a model train layout in little pieces when I have quiet time.

follow_ups.question: How often do you budget?
follow_ups.response: Weekly, usually Sunday evening.

follow_ups.question: What do you do for your back?
follow_ups.response: Stretching, light core work, and trying not to lift like an idiot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is that I have been going to the gym more regularly, about two times a week, because my back got tight after a stretch of attic jobs. I also started setting aside time to study code material instead of only learning on the job. Solar work has changed some days too because those jobs can start early and involve different equipment than normal residential calls.

follow_ups.question: When do you study?
follow_ups.response: Usually Tuesday or Thursday evening for about an hour.

follow_ups.question: Has the gym helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, as long as I keep it low impact and do not overdo it.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me. I see my younger cousins sometimes at family gatherings, but I am not responsible for a child's school routine.

follow_ups.question: Do children factor into your weekly responsibilities at all?
follow_ups.response: No, not day to day.

follow_ups.question: Do you want children later?
follow_ups.response: Maybe someday, but not soon. I want to be more financially settled first.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have been limited. I have been pulled over once for a brake light and got a warning. On job sites, inspectors are more common in my life than police, honestly. I try to keep everything boring: registration current, tools locked up, no reason for trouble.

follow_ups.question: How did that traffic stop feel?
follow_ups.response: Nervous, but it was straightforward. I fixed the light that weekend.

follow_ups.question: Do you know officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Not really, just acquaintances through community or family connections.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police around traffic accidents or neighborhood calls. Nothing personal stands out beyond that.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police?
follow_ups.response: No, I have not had to.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable doing so?
follow_ups.response: For something serious, yes, but I would rather avoid needing to.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I do not have close family who have been arrested either, at least not that I know about.

follow_ups.question: Any friends with that experience?
follow_ups.response: Not close friends.

follow_ups.question: Does that affect how you see the system?
follow_ups.response: I know my experience is pretty limited compared with other people's.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote sometimes, but I am not perfect about every local election. I voted in the last presidential election I was eligible for and try to pay attention when there are state or city issues that affect work, housing, or taxes. I feel like I should be more consistent with local races because those probably touch daily life more than people admit.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide whether to vote?
follow_ups.response: If I understand the candidates or the issue enough, I go. If I have not done the homework, I hesitate.

follow_ups.question: Do family members influence your voting?
follow_ups.response: Some, but I do not just copy them. Family conversations make me think through things.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself moderate, maybe a little conservative on spending and personal responsibility, but not extreme. I care about people being able to work, afford a place to live, and not get buried by health bills or rent. I also think trades and community colleges deserve more respect and support because not everyone needs the same path. On energy, I am interested in solar, but I look at it practically: does it work, is it safe, can normal homeowners afford it. I do not like politics when it turns into people yelling online. I am more likely to listen to someone who can explain what a policy actually does. I guess I am independent, leaning slightly Republican on some economic things, but not strongly attached to a party.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Housing costs and trade opportunities. Those affect whether someone my age can build a stable life.

follow_ups.question: What turns you off politically?
follow_ups.response: Performative arguments, especially online, where nobody is trying to solve anything.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten more interested in local policy than national arguments. When I was younger, politics felt like teams on TV. Now I notice permitting, housing, utility costs, trade licensing, and whether schools are actually preparing people for real work. I have also become more open to renewable energy incentives because I have seen customers interested in solar but worried about upfront cost.

follow_ups.question: What made local issues feel more real?
follow_ups.response: Paying rent and working on homes. You see how rules and costs affect real people.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed party identity?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I still think of myself as independent.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say somewhat. I am a white guy from a pretty stable family, so I know I have not had the same experiences some people have had with police or discrimination. The conversations made me think more about what I do not see. At the same time, I am cautious about slogans and try to separate the real issues from internet fights.

follow_ups.question: Where did you hear most about it?
follow_ups.response: News, social media clips, and conversations at work or family dinners.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: Mostly it made me listen more and talk less when I do not know enough.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think accountability matters. If a police department has bad patterns, people should not just shrug that off. I also think communities need public safety, so my instinct is more reform and standards than tearing everything down. I try to think about it practically: training, body cameras, consequences for misconduct, and treating people fairly.

follow_ups.question: Do people close to you agree?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some think the whole topic gets exaggerated. It depends who I am talking to.

follow_ups.question: Do you bring it up often?
follow_ups.response: No. I usually only talk about it if someone else brings it up.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country has made progress, but there are still real differences in opportunity and treatment. In Greensboro you are around people from different backgrounds, so it is not some abstract thing. I do not pretend to have all the answers. I mostly think people should be honest, not defensive, and willing to look at how systems work for different people.

follow_ups.question: Does your workplace shape that view?
follow_ups.response: Yes, job sites have people from different backgrounds, and you learn by working beside people.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about race with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but carefully. It can get tense if people feel accused.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly kept my thoughts private and listened. I have not joined protests. I have talked with a few coworkers and family members, but I try not to act like an expert.

follow_ups.question: Why not protest?
follow_ups.response: Big crowds are not really my thing, and I did not feel informed enough to make myself visible that way.

follow_ups.question: What do you do instead?
follow_ups.response: Read a little, listen, and try to treat people fairly in my own life.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My family is mixed in the sense that some are sympathetic and some get tired of hearing about it. My younger sister is probably more outspoken about racism than my parents. At work, guys mostly avoid politics unless it comes up during lunch. A couple coworkers have had stronger views because of their own experiences with police.

follow_ups.question: Do disagreements cause conflict?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. People might get quiet or change the subject.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you most on this?
follow_ups.response: Probably coworkers who have different life experiences than mine.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I am 21, I work a physical job, and I can do what I need to do. The main issue is lower back tightness from lifting, crawling, and awkward positions on job sites. I try to manage it with stretching, light strength training, and being smarter about how I move. I do not have any major chronic diagnosis.

follow_ups.question: How often does your back bother you?
follow_ups.response: Mildly a few times a week, worse after crawlspace or attic work.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I do not go often unless I need to.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: The job keeps me moving, which helps. What makes it hard is irregular lunches, long days, heat, and grabbing ramen or fast food when I get home late. It is easier when I meal prep and get to the gym twice a week.

follow_ups.question: What do you meal prep?
follow_ups.response: Chicken, rice, sweet potatoes, salad, or leftovers from family dinners.

follow_ups.question: What gets in the way most?
follow_ups.response: Being tired after work.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No major diagnosis or broken bones. The biggest thing was a back flare-up after several days of attic work in summer heat. It was not dramatic, but I had trouble bending for a few days and realized I needed to take prevention seriously. Since then I have been more careful about stretching and asking for help with awkward lifts.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care once just to make sure it was not something worse.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect work?
follow_ups.response: For a couple days I moved slower and avoided heavy lifting.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My back can get in the way if I ignore it, but it has not stopped me from working long term. I do not have children to care for.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for it?
follow_ups.response: Only a partial day once.

follow_ups.question: What prevents it from getting worse?
follow_ups.response: Better lifting, stretching, and not trying to prove anything.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: A little. My grandparents have normal aging issues, and one has blood pressure problems. My parents handle most appointments, but I help with small repairs, rides, or errands when asked. It makes me aware that family responsibility builds over time.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, depending on what is needed.

follow_ups.question: Does it stress you?
follow_ups.response: Some, but it also feels like what family does.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have not had to fully forgo care, but cost definitely makes me think twice. I use insurance through work, though the benefits are not amazing. For something small, I might wait and see instead of making an appointment. My family is similar: they go when they need to, but everybody watches the bills.

follow_ups.question: What care do you delay?
follow_ups.response: Mostly minor stuff like back soreness unless it feels serious.

follow_ups.question: Do you have dental care?
follow_ups.response: Basic, but I am careful because dental bills add up fast.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal. My family does some home remedies, like tea, soup, heat packs, stretching, and my grandmother's advice about food and rest. For my back I use heat and stretching before I would call it alternative medicine.

follow_ups.question: Any supplements?
follow_ups.response: Just normal vitamins sometimes, nothing serious.

follow_ups.question: Would you try chiropractic care?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, but I would want someone reputable and not too expensive.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink lightly, maybe a beer during a game or at a family gathering. When I am stressed, I am more likely to go quiet, work on wood, play a record, or go fishing than drink heavily.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a week or less.

follow_ups.question: Any vaping?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other drugs. If my back hurts, I might take ibuprofen with food and use a heating pad. The most recent time was after a long day pulling wire overhead; I took ibuprofen that night and stretched before bed.

follow_ups.question: Any prescription pain meds?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Do coworkers use substances to cope?
follow_ups.response: Some drink or use weed, but I keep away from that as a habit.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I use my work insurance and pay copays when I have to. My parents have their own coverage. For my grandparents, Medicare is part of it, and family helps with transportation or errands more than direct bills. We are not in crisis, but nobody treats health care like it is cheap.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep emergency savings for health costs?
follow_ups.response: Yes, that is one reason I try to save.

follow_ups.question: What worries you most?
follow_ups.response: A big unexpected bill.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally fine with vaccines. I am not excited about shots, but I think routine vaccination makes sense, especially if doctors recommend it.

follow_ups.question: Did COVID affect your view?
follow_ups.response: It made me pay more attention, but I tried not to get pulled into online arguments.

follow_ups.question: Do you get flu shots?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, not every year.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my doctor most. I also look at CDC information if I need something official, but I prefer asking a medical person because online searching can get messy fast. I do not rely on social media for medical decisions.

follow_ups.question: Do family opinions matter?
follow_ups.response: They matter personally, but I still want medical advice.

follow_ups.question: Do you read news about health?
follow_ups.response: Only when something directly affects me.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: I have been mostly steady, but tired. Work can wear me down, and I put pressure on myself to stay on track with licensing and saving money. I am not someone who talks about feelings easily, so stress comes out as getting quiet or overworking. The good parts are that I feel like I have direction. When I get outdoors or work on a table in the garage, I feel more like myself.

follow_ups.question: What does a bad week look like?
follow_ups.response: Long job days, messy apartment, no gym, eating ramen, and feeling behind on everything.

follow_ups.question: What helps reset you?
follow_ups.response: Fishing early, putting on Pink Floyd or Zeppelin, and cleaning up my space.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last summer I had a rough stretch where work was hot, my back hurt, and I felt like I was not moving fast enough toward my goals. I came home one Friday and just sat in my truck for a while because I did not want to go inside and deal with anything. The next morning I drove out early to fish, no music, no phone much, just quiet. It did not fix everything, but it slowed me down enough to make a plan instead of stewing.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell anyone?
follow_ups.response: I told my dad a little, but not the full emotional part.

follow_ups.question: What plan did you make?
follow_ups.response: Gym twice a week, stop skipping meals, and study in smaller chunks.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would not say I have been diagnosed with depression or anxiety. I do get anxious about money, doing work right, and whether I am falling behind. It is manageable, but I know I can bottle things up. Routine helps me a lot.

follow_ups.question: Have you considered counseling?
follow_ups.response: Not seriously, but I would not rule it out if things got worse.

follow_ups.question: How do you know stress is building?
